# Exponential dispersion models {#sec-exponential}

This chapter introduces a class of response distributions more general than 
the normal distribution, which  will 
form the basis of an extension of the linear model in @sec-generalized-linear. 
Among the possible 
alternatives to the normal distribution are discrete distributions like the binomial and the Poisson 
distribution and continuous distributions like the Gamma distribution.

## A motivating example

To motivate the introduction of the exponential dispersion models, we consider an example. 

\index{Bernoulli model}

::: {#exm-bernoulli}

## Bernoulli model

For a binary response variable $Y \in \{0, 1\}$ with $p = \mathbf{P}(Y = 1)$ 
the log-odds parameter is \index{log-odds}
$$
    \theta \coloneqq \log \frac{\mathbf{P}(Y = 1)}{\mathbf{P}(Y = 0)} = \log \frac{p}{1 - p}.
$$
Rearranging this equation gives 
$$
    p = \frac{e^{\theta}}{1 + e^{\theta}} \qquad \text{and} \qquad
    1 - p = \frac{1}{1 + e^{\theta}}.
$$
From this,
$$
    \mathbf{P}(Y = y) = p^y(1-p)^{(1-y)} = \frac{e^{y\theta}}{1 + e^{\theta}}
$$
for $y \in \{0, 1\}.$ The probability mass function thus takes the form 
$$
    \frac{1}{c(\theta)}e^{y \theta}
$$ 
with $c(\theta) = 1 + e^{\theta}.$ By direct computations we may observe that 
$$
    \mathbf{E}(Y) = p = \frac{c'(\theta)}{c(\theta)} = (\log c(\theta))'
$$
and that 
$$
    \mathbf{V}(Y) = p(1-p) = \left(\frac{c'(\theta)}{c(\theta)}\right)'.
$$
That is, the mean can be found by differentiation of $\log c,$ and the 
variance is the derivative of the mean as a function of $\theta.$ 
::: 

The identities relating the mean, variance and 
log-odds parameter $\theta$  for the Bernoulli model above may seem coincidental for this
particular model. In fact, they are examples from the general theory 
of exponential families. The Bernoulli model can be parametrized by 
the mean value parameter (the probability $p$) or the log-odds parameter $\theta.$ The
function
$$
    \theta \mapsto \frac{e^{\theta}}{1 + e^{\theta}} = p
$$ 
is a one-to-one correspondence mapping $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,1).$ The inverse of
this function is the *logit function* \index{logit function}
$$
    \mathrm{logit}(p) = \log \frac{p}{1 - p}.
$$
Moreover, the variance can be expressed in terms of the mean as $p(1-p)$
or in terms of the log-odds parameter. The latter is obtainable from the function 
$c$ via differentiation. 

As mentioned, the Bernoulli model is an example of a univariate exponential family. The normal
distribution with fixed variance is another example. 
This chapter investigates the class of exponential families on the real line with 
the extension that a dispersion parameter is also allowed. By introducing a 
dispersion parameter the resulting class of exponential dispersion models includes a 
number of two-parameter families of distributions on the real line such as the 
normal distribution and the Gamma distribution. 

## Exponential dispersion models

An exponential dispersion model is a two-parameter family of 
so-called exponential dispersion distributions determined by an exponential family 
and a dispersion parameter. The theory of exponential dispersion models provides a framework for a number 
of widely applied univariate distributions. The theory is interesting in itself, but 
it is treated here first of all to provide the theoretical foundation for
generalized linear regression models as treated in @sec-generalized-linear. In this section the models and their associated terminology are introduced, and the general relation between mean and 
variance is established. In subsequent chapters the statistical theory 
for generalized linear models is developed based on the framework of exponential 
dispersion models. 

Every model is determined by a single $\sigma$-finite measure on the real line. 
With $\nu$ a $\sigma$-finite measure on $\mathbb{R}$ we define 
$c : \mathbb{R} \to [0,\infty]$ by 
$$      
    c(\theta) = \int e^{\theta y} \, \nu(\mathrm{d} y),
$$ {#eq-psidef}
and we let
$$ 
    I = \{ \theta \in \mathbb{R} \mid c(\theta) < \infty \}^{\circ}
$$
denote the interior of the set of $\theta$-s for which $c(\theta) < \infty.$ 

Note that it is possible that $I = \emptyset$---take, for instance, $\nu$ to be Lebesgue measure.
If $\nu$ is a finite measure then $c(0) < \infty,$
but it is still possible that $c(\theta) = \infty$ for all $\theta \neq 0,$ which results 
in $I = \emptyset.$ The case where $I$ is empty is not of any relevance. There are two 
other special situations that are not relevant either. If $\nu$ is the zero measure, $c(\theta) = 0,$ 
and if $\nu$ is a one-point measure, that is, $\nu = a \delta_{y}$ for $a \in (0, \infty)$ and $\delta_y$ the Dirac 
measure in $y,$ then $c(\theta) = a e^{\theta y}.$ Neither of these two cases will 
be of any interest, and they result in pathological problems that we want to avoid. 
We will therefore make the following regularity assumptions about $\nu$ throughout. 

* The measure $\nu$ is not the zero measure, nor is it a one-point measure. 
* The open set $I$ is non-empty.
 
By the assumption that $\nu$ is not the zero measure, it follows that $c(\theta) > 0$ for
$\theta \in I.$ This makes the following definition possible.

\index{exponential family} \index{canonical parameter!exponential family} \index{structure measure}

::: {#def-exponential-family}
The exponential family with 
structure measure $\nu$ is the one-parameter family of probability measures, $P_{\theta}$ for $\theta \in I,$  defined by
$$
    \frac{\mathrm{d} P_\theta}{\mathrm{d} \nu}(y) = \frac{1}{c(\theta)}e^{\theta y}.
$$
The parameter $\theta$ is called the canonical parameter. 
:::

Note that the exponential family is determined completely by the choice of the structure 
measure $\nu.$ Introducing $\kappa(\theta) = \log c(\theta)$ we have that 
$$
    \frac{\mathrm{d} P_\theta}{\mathrm{d} \nu}(y) = e^{\theta y - \kappa(\theta)}
$$
for $\theta \in I.$ The function $\kappa$ is called the *unit cumulant function*
\index{cumulant function!unit}
for the exponential family. It is closely related to the cumulant generating functions 
for the probability measures in the exponential family, see @exr-cum.

Under the regularity assumptions we have made on $\nu$ we can obtain a 
couple of very useful results about the exponential family. 

::: {#lem-Istruct}
The set $I$ is an open interval, the parametrization  $\theta \mapsto P_{\theta}$ is 
one-to-one, and the function $\kappa : I \mapsto \mathbb{R}$ is strictly convex. 
::: 

::: {.proof}
We first prove that the parametrization is one-to-one. If $P_{\theta_1} = P_{\theta_2}$
their densities w.r.t. $\nu$ must agree $\nu$-almost everywhere, which implies that
$$(\theta_1 - \theta_2)y = \kappa(\theta_1) - \kappa(\theta_2)$$
for $\nu$-almost all $y.$ Since $\nu$ is assumed not to be the zero measure or a one-point measure, 
this can only hold if $\theta_1 = \theta_2.$ 

To prove that $I$ is an interval let $\theta_1, \theta_2 \in I,$ and let $\alpha \in (0, 1).$ Then by Hölder's inequality
$$
\begin{align*}
c(\alpha \theta_1 + (1-\alpha)\theta_2) & = \int e^{\alpha \theta_1 y} e^{(1-\alpha)\theta_2 y}  \, \nu(\mathrm{d} y) \\
& \leq   \left(\int e^{\theta_1 y} \, \nu(\mathrm{d} y)\right)^{\alpha} \left(\int e^{\theta_2 y}  \, \nu(\mathrm{d} y)\right)^{1-\alpha} \\
& = c(\theta_1)^{\alpha} c(\theta_2)^{1-\alpha} < \infty.
\end{align*}
$$
This proves that $I$ is an interval. It is by definition open. 
[Hölder's inequality says that 
$$
    \int|fg|  \leq \left(\int |f|^p\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}\left(\int |g|^q\right)^{\frac{1}{q}}
$$
for $p,q \geq 1$ and $\frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{q} = 1.$ It is used with 
$$
\begin{align*}
f(y) & = e^{\alpha \theta_1 y}, \\
g(y) &= & e^{(1-\alpha)\theta_2 y},
\end{align*}
$$
$$
    p = \frac{1}{\alpha} \ \mathrm{ and } \ q = \frac{1}{1-\alpha}.
$$
]{.aside}
Finally, it follows directly from the inequality above that 
$$
    \kappa(\alpha \theta_1 + (1-\alpha) \theta_2) \leq \alpha \kappa(\theta_1) + (1-\alpha)\kappa(\theta_2),
$$
which shows that $\kappa$ is convex. If we have equality in this inequality, we have equality in Hölder's inequality.
This happens only if $e^{\theta_1 y}/c(\theta_1) = e^{\theta_2 y}/c(\theta_2)$ for $\nu$-almost all $y,$ 
and just as above we conclude that this implies $\theta_1 = \theta_2.$ The conclusion is that $\kappa$ is
strictly convex. 
::: 

The structure measure $\nu$ determines the unit cumulant function by the formula
$$
    \kappa(\theta) = \log \int e^{\theta y} \, \nu(\mathrm{d}y).
$$
The fact that $I$ is open implies that $\kappa$ determines $\nu$ uniquely, see
@exr-uniqueness. 

It turns out that a number of univariate exponential families 
can be embedded in a two-parameter family of probability 
measures with a common structure. This embedding exists when 
the structure measure belongs to a family of $\sigma$-finite measures $\nu_{\varphi}$ parametrized by $\varphi > 0,$ whose 
cumulant functions are $\theta \mapsto \kappa(\varphi \theta)/\varphi.$ 

It is not at all obvious whether there exists a 
$\sigma$-finite measure $\nu_{\varphi}$ with cumulant function $\kappa(\varphi \theta)/\varphi$ for a given unit cumulant function $\kappa.$ \index{cumulant function!with dispersion parameter}
We will find this to be the case for all $\varphi > 0$ for several concrete examples, but 
there are examples, such as the Bernoulli model, where the extension is
only possible for $\varphi^{-1} \in \mathbb{N}$. We will not pursue a systematic study, 
but see [@jorgensen1997theory, Chapter 4].

When the extension is possible, we have $\nu_1 = \nu$ and 
$$
    \frac{\kappa(\varphi \theta)}{\varphi} = \log \int e^{\theta y} \, \nu_{\varphi}(\mathrm{d}y).
$$
Changing parameter from $\varphi \theta$ to $\theta$, we can rewrite the above identity as
$$
    \frac{\kappa(\theta)}{\varphi} = \log \int e^{\frac{\theta y}{\varphi}} \, \nu_{\varphi}(\mathrm{d}y)
    = \log \int e^{\theta y} \, \bar{\nu}_{\varphi}(\mathrm{d}y),
$$
where $\bar{\nu}_{\varphi}$ is a scale transformation of $\nu_\varphi$. 
Since these cumulant functions are defined on the same open interval $I$ as $\kappa$, they uniquely determine
$\bar{\nu}_{\varphi}$, and thus $\nu_\varphi$, for all $\varphi > 0$ by @exr-uniqueness. The extension of the structure measure 
$\nu$ to the family $\nu_{\varphi}$ for $\varphi > 0$ is therefore unique---if there exists such an extension---and all
the measures $\nu_{\varphi}$ and $\bar{\nu}_{\varphi}$ 
satisfy the same regularity conditions we have required of $\nu.$ 

Whenever $\nu$ is embedded in such a family $(\nu_{\varphi})_{\varphi > 0}$ of structure measures 
we introduce the *exponential dispersion model* determined by $\nu$---
a two-parameter family of probability measures---by
$$
    \frac{\mathrm{d} P_{\theta, \varphi}}{\mathrm{d} \nu_{\varphi}} (y) = e^{\frac{\theta y - \kappa(\theta)}{\varphi}}.
$$ {#eq-expdisp}
The parameter $\varphi$ is called the dispersion parameter, and we call $\nu = \nu_1$ the 
unit structure measure for the exponential dispersion model. 

For fixed $\varphi$ 
the exponential dispersion model is an exponential family with 
structure measure $\nu_{\varphi}$ and canonical parameter $\theta/\varphi.$ 
[The parameters $\varphi$ and $\theta$ are only uniquely determined up to a scale transformation, which 
corresponds to specifying which of the structure measures $\nu_{\varphi}$ is the unit structure measure.]{.aside}
\index{canonical parameter!exponential dispersion model} \index{structure measure!unit} We 
abuse the terminology slightly and call $\theta$ the canonical parameter for the 
exponential dispersion model. Thus, whether $\theta/\varphi$ or $\theta$ is 
canonical depends upon whether we regard the model as an exponential family with structure measure $\nu_{\varphi}$
or as an exponential dispersion model with unit structure measure $\nu.$ Whenever we consider 
an exponential dispersion model, the measure $\nu$ will always denote the unit structure measure $\nu_1.$ 

\index{exponential dispersion distribution}

::: {#def-expdisp}
The probability distribution $P_{\theta, \varphi}$ is called the 
$(\theta, \nu_{\varphi})$-exponential dispersion distribution and is 
denoted $\mathcal{E}(\theta, \nu_{\varphi}).$ 
::: 

In practice we check that a given parametrized family of distributions is, in fact, an exponential dispersion model
by checking that its density can be brought on the form ([-@eq-expdisp]). 

\index{distribution!normal}

::: {#exm-normal}
The normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(\mu, 1)$ has density 
$$
    \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac{(y-\mu)^2}{2}} = e^{y\mu -
    \frac{\mu^2}{2}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}  e^{-\frac{y^2}{2}}
$$
w.r.t. Lebesgue measure $m.$ We identify this as an
exponential family with[^unique]
$$
    \theta = \mu, \quad \kappa(\theta) = \frac{\theta^2}{2} \quad \mathrm{and} \quad
    \frac{\mathrm{d}\nu}{\mathrm{d} m}(y) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}  e^{-\frac{y^2}{2}}.
$$
Thus the structure measure $\nu$ is the standard normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$.

Introducing a dispersion parameter $\varphi > 0$ we observe that  
$$
    \frac{\kappa(\theta)}{\varphi} = \frac{1}{\varphi}\frac{\theta^2}{2} = \frac{(\theta/\sqrt{\varphi})^2}{2} 
    = \log \int e^{\frac{\theta y}{\sqrt{\varphi}}} \nu(\mathrm{d}y) 
    = \log \int e^{\frac{\theta y}{\varphi}} \nu_\varphi(\mathrm{d}y)
$$
where $\nu_\varphi$ is a scale transformation[^scale] of $\nu$. That is, $\nu_\varphi$ is 
the $\mathcal{N}(0, \varphi)$ distribution with 
$$
    \frac{\mathrm{d} \nu_{\varphi}}{\mathrm{d} m}(y) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi \varphi}} e^{-\frac{y^2}{2\varphi}}.
$$
The corresponding exponential dispersion distribution is $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \varphi)$. 
With the notation introduced in @def-expdisp,
$$
    \mathcal{E}\left(\mu, \nu_{\sigma^2} \right) = \mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2),
$$
where we, as is usual for the normal distribution, denote the dispersion 
parameter by $\sigma^2$. 

[^unique]: The $\kappa$ and $\nu$ are not unique. The constant $$\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}$$ in $\nu$ can be moved to a $- \log \sqrt{2\pi}$ term in $\kappa.$

[^scale]: With $S_{\sigma}(x) = \sigma x$ denoting a scale transformation, $\nu_{\varphi} = S_{\sqrt{\varphi}}(\nu).$ 

:::


\index{distribution!Poisson}


::: {#exm-pois}
The Poisson distribution with mean $\mu > 0$ has density (probability mass function)
$$e^{-\mu} \frac{\mu^y}{y!}$$
w.r.t. the counting measure $\tau$ for $y \in \mathbb{N}_0.$ With $\theta = \log \mu$ we can rewrite this density as
$$e^{y \log \mu -\mu} \frac{1}{y!} = e^{y \theta - e^{\theta}} \frac{1}{y!},$$
and we identify the distribution as an exponential family with 
$$\theta = \log \mu, \quad \kappa(\theta) = e^{\theta} \quad \mathrm{and} \quad  \frac{\mathrm{d}\nu}{\mathrm{d} \tau} (y) = \frac{1}{y!}.$$
We conclude that 
$$\mathcal{E}\left(\log \mu, \frac{1}{y!} \cdot \tau \right) = \mathrm{Pois}(\mu).$$
[It is possible to introduce a dispersion parameter via 
a scaled Poisson distribution, see @exr-poisson-disp, but the resulting distribution will 
only have integer support if $\varphi \in \mathbb{N}$. It is therefore not 
useful in general for modeling counts.]{.aside}
:::

The next example is the $\Gamma$-family of distributions, whose representation as an 
exponential dispersion model is less obvious. These distributions can be 
parametrized by a shape and a scale parameter, and we have to rewrite their density 
to identify the parametrization in terms of the canonical parameter and the 
dispersion parameter. For this family of distributions there is yet another useful 
parametrization in terms of mean and variance. 

\index{gamma distribution} \index{distribution!gamma}

::: {#exm-gam}
The $\Gamma$-distribution with shape parameter $\lambda > 0$ 
and scale parameter $\alpha > 0$ has density 
$$
    \frac{1}{\alpha^{\lambda} \Gamma(\lambda)} y^{\lambda - 1} e^{-y/\alpha} = 
    e^{\frac{- y/(\lambda \alpha) - \log (\lambda \alpha)}{1/\lambda}} 
    \frac{\lambda^{\lambda}}{\Gamma(\lambda)} y^{\lambda - 1} 
$$
w.r.t. Lebesgue measure $m$ on $(0, \infty).$ We identify this family of 
distributions as the exponential dispersion model with dispersion parameter 
$\varphi = 1/\lambda,$ canonical parameter 
$$
    \theta = - 1 /(\lambda \alpha)  < 0,
$$ 
$$
    \kappa(\theta) =  - \log (- \theta),
$$
and structure measure given by
$$
    \frac{\mathrm{d} \nu_{\varphi}}{\mathrm{d} m}  = 
    \frac{1}{\varphi^{1/\varphi}\Gamma(1/\varphi)} y^{\frac{1}{\varphi} - 1}
$$
on $(0, \infty).$ We have $I = (- \infty, 0).$ 
The mean value of the $\Gamma$-distribution is 
$\mu = \alpha \lambda = - \frac{1}{\theta},$ and the variance is 
$\alpha^2 \lambda = \varphi \mu^2 = \varphi/\theta^2.$ 
Observe that the unit structure measure, $\nu_1,$ is
Lebesgue measure on $(0, \infty),$ and the corresponding exponential family 
is the exponential distribution. 
:::

The next theorem shows that the mean and variance for exponential dispersion models 
are always computable via differentiation of the cumulant function. 

[For the $\Gamma$-distribution:
$$
    \kappa'(\theta) = - \frac{1}{\theta}
$$ 
and 
$$
    \kappa''(\theta) = \frac{1}{\theta^2}.
$$
]{.aside}

::: {#thm-meanvar}
The function $\kappa$ is infinitely often differentiable on $I.$ If 
$Y \sim \mathcal{E}(\theta, \nu_{\varphi})$ for $\theta \in I$ then 
$$
    \mathbf{E}(Y) = \kappa'(\theta)
$$ {#eq-kapmean}
and
$$
    \mathbf{V}(Y) = \varphi \kappa''(\theta).
$$ {#eq-kapvar}
::: 

::: {.proof}  
It follows by 
a suitable domination argument that, for $\theta \in I,$ 
$$
    \frac{\mathrm{d}^n}{\mathrm{d}\theta^n} c(\theta) = \int y^n e^{\theta y} \, \nu(\mathrm{d} y) = c(\theta) \mathbf{E}(Y^n).
$$
Since $\kappa(\theta) = \log c(\theta),$ it follows that also $\kappa$ is infinitely often differentiable. 
In particular, if $Y \sim \mathcal{E}(\theta, \nu_1),$
$$
    \mathbf{E}(Y) = \frac{c'(\theta)}{c(\theta)} = (\log c)'(\theta) = \kappa'(\theta),
$$
and 
$$
    \mathbf{E}(Y^2) =  \frac{c''(\theta)}{c(\theta)},
$$
and we find that 
$$
    \mathbf{V}(Y) = \mathbf{E}(Y^2) - (\mathbf{E}(Y))^2 =  \frac{c''(\theta)c(\theta) - c'(\theta)^2}{c(\theta)^2} = \kappa''(\theta).
$$
The general case for $\varphi \neq 1$ can be proved by similar arguments. 
Alternatively, observe that for an arbitrary dispersion parameter
$\varphi > 0,$ the distribution of $Y$ is an exponential family with canonical parameter $\theta_0 = \theta/\varphi$
and with corresponding cumulant function
$$
    \kappa_0(\theta_0) = \frac{\kappa(\varphi \theta_0)}{\varphi}.
$$ 
The conclusion follows by differentiating $\kappa_0$ twice w.r.t. $\theta_0.$ 
:::

We know from @lem-Istruct that $\kappa$ is strictly convex. Since $\kappa$ 
was found to be differentiable on $I,$ this implies that $\kappa'$ is a strictly increasing function. 
This can also be seen directly from the previous theorem. Indeed, by the regularity assumptions on $\nu_{\varphi},$ 
$P_{\theta, \varphi}$ is not a Dirac measure, which implies that $\mathbf{V}(Y) > 0$ in ([-@eq-kapvar]), see 
@exr-deg.
Hence $\kappa''$ is strictly positive, and it follows that $\kappa'$ is strictly increasing, and that 
$\kappa$ is strictly convex. 
[Theorem @thm-meanvar only implies that $\kappa$ is (strictly) convex because $I$ is 
already known to be an interval. The argument based on Hölder's inequality 
is necessary to show this.]{.aside}

That $\kappa'$ is continuous and strictly increasing imply that the range of $\kappa',$ 
$$
    J \coloneqq \kappa'(I),
$$ 
is an open interval. This range 
is the range of possible mean values for the exponential dispersion model. 
Since $\kappa'$ bijectively maps $I$ onto $J$ we can always express the variance in terms of 
the mean. 

\index{Variance function}

::: {#def-variance-function}
The variance function $\mathcal{V} : J \to (0, \infty)$ is defined as
$$\mathcal{V}(\mu) = \kappa''((\kappa')^{-1}(\mu)).$$
::: 

From the considerations above, the map 
$$
    (\theta, \varphi) \mapsto (\kappa'(\theta), \varphi \kappa''(\theta)) = (\mu, \varphi \mathcal{V}(\mu))
$$
is a bijection from $I \times (0, \infty)$ onto $J \times (0,\infty),$ 
and this shows that the exponential dispersion model can be parametrized either 
in terms of the canonical and dispersion parameters or in terms of the mean and variance.  

\index{arbitrary parametrization}

Occasionally, a third parametrization exists of an exponential 
dispersion model that may be useful or even natural, depending 
on the model.  
With $H \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $\theta : H \to I,$ the canonical 
parameter, $\theta(\eta),$ is in such cases expressed in terms of 
an *arbitrary* parameter $\eta \in H.$ We call $\eta$ arbitrary because we do not
make any assumptions about what this parameter is\sidenote{In regression applications, $\eta$ will be $X^T \beta,$ known as the linear predictor, \index{linear predictor} for a vector of predictors $X.$}, 
besides that it parametrizes the exponential dispersion model. The density for the exponential dispersion model 
w.r.t. $\nu_{\varphi}$ in the arbitrary parametrization is 
$$
    e^{\frac{\theta(\eta)y - \zeta(\eta)}{\varphi}}
$$
where $\zeta(\eta) = \kappa(\theta(\eta))$ and $\eta \in H.$ 
The parametrization, $\eta \mapsto \theta(\eta)$, is allowed to 
depend upon additional (nuisance) parameters. 
We suppress any such dependences in the abstract notation. It is, however, not allowed 
to depend upon the dispersion parameter[^var-ind], because then the dispersion parameter 
cannot be eliminated from subsequent estimation equations. 

[^var-ind]: In technical terms, the dispersion parameter must be *variation independent* of nuisance parameters entering $\eta \mapsto \theta(\eta)$.

The *mean value function*, in the arbitrary parametrization, is 
given as
$$
    \mu(\eta) = \kappa'(\theta(\eta)).
$$
We can then express the mean and the variance functions in terms of the function $\eta \mapsto \zeta(\eta).$

::: {#cor-meanvar}
If $\theta$ is twice differentiable as a function of $\eta$ with $\theta'(\eta) \neq 0,$ then  
$$
    \mu(\eta) = \frac{\zeta'(\eta)}{\theta'(\eta)}
$$
and 
$$
    \mathcal{V}(\mu(\eta)) = \frac{\zeta''(\eta)\theta'(\eta) - \zeta'(\eta)\theta''(\eta)}{\theta'(\eta)^3} 
= \frac{\mu'(\eta)}{\theta'(\eta)}.
$$
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-diagram-1
#| fig-cap: "Relations between the three parametrizations."
#| column: margin
#| engine: tikz
#| echo: false
\begin{tikzpicture}[description/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt}] 
\matrix (m) [matrix of math nodes, row sep=4em, column sep=5em, text height=1.5ex, text depth=0.25ex] {
 J & H \\
 I & \\}; 
\path[->] 
(m-1-2) edge node [above] {$\mu$} (m-1-1) 
(m-2-1) edge node [left] {$\kappa'$} (m-1-1)
(m-1-2) edge node [below] {$\theta$} (m-2-1);
\end{tikzpicture}
```

::: {.proof}
From the definition $\zeta(\eta) = \kappa(\theta(\eta))$ we get by differentiation 
and ([-@eq-kapmean]) that 
$$\zeta'(\eta) = \kappa'(\theta(\eta)) \theta'(\eta) = \mu(\eta) \theta'(\eta),$$
and the first identity follows. An additional differentiation yields
$$
\begin{align*}
\zeta''(\eta) & = \kappa''(\theta(\eta)) \theta'(\eta)^2 +  \kappa'(\theta(\eta)) \theta''(\eta) \\
& = \mathcal{V}(\mu(\eta)) \theta'(\eta)^2 +  \frac{\zeta'(\eta) \theta''(\eta)}{\theta'(\eta)},
\end{align*}
$$
and the second identity follows by isolating $\mathcal{V}(\mu(\eta)).$ 
:::

::: {#exm-gammaloglink}
The canonical parameter in the $\Gamma$-model can be parametrized by 
$H = \mathbb{R}$ via the parametrization 
$$
    \theta(\eta) = - e^{-\eta}.
$$
Then $\zeta(\eta) = \eta$ and from @cor-meanvar it follows that 
$$
    \mu(\eta) = e^{\eta}.
$$
::: 


When the mean value function, defined above as a function of the arbitrary parameter, 
is bijective, its inverse is called *the link function* and denoted $g.$ \index{link function}
It maps the mean value $\mu$ to the arbitrary parameter $\eta,$ that is, 
$$
    \eta = g(\mu).
$$ 
The choice of the link function (equivalently, the mean value function) completely 
determines the $\theta$-map and vice versa. The choice for which 
$\theta = \eta$ plays a particularly central role. If $\theta = \eta$ then $\mu = \kappa',$
and the corresponding link function is $g = (\kappa')^{-1}.$ 

\index{canonical link function} \index{link function!canonical} 

::: {#def-canonical-link}
The canonical link function is the link function 
$$
    g = (\kappa')^{-1}.
$$
[The variance function is 
$$
    \mathcal{V}(\mu) = \kappa''(g(\mu))
$$ 
in terms of the canonical link $g$.]{.aside}
::: 

::: {#exm-pois-model} 
For the Poisson distribution we have $\kappa(\theta) = e^{\theta},$ 
see @exm-pois. This implies that $\kappa'(\theta) = e^{\theta}$ and the canonical 
link function is, for the Poisson distribution, $g(\mu) = \log \mu.$ 
::: 

A regression model with $\eta = X^T \beta$ and a log-link function is \index{log-linear}
often called a log-linear model. Thus the canonical link function for the 
Poisson distribution gives a log-linear regression model. @exm-gammaloglink
gives a log-linear regression model with a $\Gamma$-distributed response, but the 
log-link is not the canonical link for the $\Gamma$-distribution as the following example will reveal. 

::: {#exm-gamma}
For the $\Gamma$-model we have from @exm-gam
that $\kappa(\theta) = - \log(-\theta)$ and
$$\kappa'(\theta) = -\frac{1}{\theta}.$$
This gives that the canonical link function for the $\Gamma$-model is 
$$g(\mu) = - \frac{1}{\mu}.$$
The canonical link for the $\Gamma$-model is not that attractive. Its range is 
$I = (-\infty, 0),$ and not the entire real line, which can be a nuisance. In practice, 
the $\Gamma$-model is often used with the log-link instead. 
::: 

```{r}
#| label: fig-diagram
#| fig-cap: "The linear predictor enters the exponential dispersion model through the mean value function."
#| column: margin
#| engine: tikz
#| echo: false
\begin{tikzpicture}[description/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt}] 
\matrix (m) [matrix of math nodes, row sep=4em, column sep=5em, text height=1.5ex, text depth=0.25ex] {
 \mu & \eta\\
 \theta & \beta \\}; 
\path[->] 
(m-1-2) edge [bend right] node [above] {$\mu$} (m-1-1) 
(m-1-1) edge [bend right] node [below] {$g$} (m-1-2) 
(m-2-1) edge node [left] {$\kappa'$} (m-1-1)
(m-1-2) edge [bend left] node [below] {$\theta$} (m-2-1)
(m-2-2) edge [bend right] node [right] {$X^T$} (m-1-2);
\end{tikzpicture}
```


In generalized linear regression models, the response distribution 
will be specified in terms of the linear predictor $\eta = X^T \beta,$ that 
determines the mean, and an exponential 
dispersion model, that determines the remaining aspects of the distribution. 
The specification of the mean is given in terms of the mean value 
function, or equivalently in terms of the link function. That is, with link function $g,$  
$$
    g(\mathbf{E}(Y \mid X)) = \eta = X^T \beta
$$
or 
$$
    \mathbf{E}(Y \mid X) = \mu(\eta).
$$
This specifies implicitly the canonical parameter in the exponential dispersion model,
and results in a model with 
$$
    \mathbf{V}(Y \mid X) = \varphi \mathcal{V}(\mu(\eta))
$$
where $\mathcal{V}$ is the variance function.

## Deviance {#sec-deviance}

\index{deviance}

The (unit) *deviance* for an exponential dispersion 
model generalizes the squared error 
$$
    (y - \mu)^2
$$
for the $\mathcal{N}(\mu, 1)$ distribution. 
For a unit cumulant function $\kappa : I \to \mathbb{R}$ we let 
$$
    \ell_y(\theta) = \theta y - \kappa(\theta)
$$
for $y \in \overline{J}$ and $\theta \in I$ denote the log-likelihood of the 
corresponding exponential family, see also 
@lem-scorefisher in @sec-generalized-linear. \index{likelihood!deviance}
The deviance is defined as twice the negative log-likelihood up to an additive 
constant. In terms of the canonical parameter the *deviance* is defined as
$$
    2 \left( \sup_{\theta_0 \in I} \ell_y(\theta_0) - \ell_y(\theta)\right)
$$
for $y \in \overline{J}$ and $\theta \in I.$ The supremum 
in the definition is attained in $g(y)$ for $y \in J$ where $g = (\kappa')^{-1}$ is the canonical link. 
For practical computations it is more convenient to express the deviance in terms of the 
mean value parameter than the canonical parameter.

\index{exponential dispersion model!deviance} \index{deviance!unit}

::: {#def-exp-deviance}
With $g$ denoting the canonical link function, the unit[^unit] 
deviance is defined as 
$$
    d(y, \mu) = 2 \left( \sup_{\mu_0 \in J} \Big\{ g(\mu_0) y - \kappa(g(\mu_0)) \Big\} -  
    g(\mu) y + \kappa(g(\mu)) \right)
$$
for $y \in \overline{J}$ and $\mu \in J.$ 
:::

[^unit]: Here *unit* refers to the dispersion parameter being 1.



For $y \in J,$ the supremum is attained in $\mu_0 = y$ and the unit deviance can
be expressed as 
$$
    d(y, \mu) = 2 \left( y (g(y) - g(\mu)) - \kappa(g(y)) + \kappa(g(\mu)) \right).
$$ {#eq-exp-deviance}
Note that by the definition of the unit deviance we have that $d(y, y) = 0$ and 
 $$
    d(y, \mu) > 0
$$
for $\mu \neq y.$ 
 
The deviance has simple analytic expressions for many concrete examples,
which are interpretable as measures of how the observation $y$ 
deviates from the expectation $\mu.$ 

\index{deviance!normal}

::: {#exm-normal-deviance}
For the normal distribution the canonical link is the identity and 
$\kappa(\theta) = \theta^2/2,$ hence 
$$d(y, \mu) = 2(y ( y - \mu) - y^2/2 + \mu^2/2) = (y - \mu)^2.$$ 
:::

\index{deviance!Poisson}

::: {#exm-pois-deviance}
For the Poisson distribution the canonical link is the logarithm,
and $\kappa(\theta) = e^{\theta},$ hence 
$$d(y, \mu) = 2(y(\log y - \log \mu) - y + \mu) = 2 ( y \log (y/\mu) - (y - \mu))$$
for $y, \mu > 0.$ It is clear from the definition that $d(0, \mu) = 2\mu,$ and the 
identity above can be maintained even for $y = 0$ by the convention $0 \log 0 = 0.$ 
:::

\index{deviance!binomial}

::: {#exm-bindev}
For the binomial distribution it follows directly from the 
definition that for $y = 1, \ldots, m - 1$ and $\mu \in (0, m)$
$$
\begin{align*}
d(y, \mu) & = 2 \Big( y \log y/m + (m-y) \log (1 - y/m) \\
& \hskip 1cm - y \log \mu/m - (m - y) \log (1 - \mu/m) \Big) \\
& = 2 \Big( y \log(y/\mu) + (m - y) \log \big( (m - y)/(m - \mu) \big) \Big).
\end{align*}
$$
Again, by the convention $0 \log 0 = 0$ the identity is seen to extend also to 
the extreme cases $y = 0$ or $y = m.$ 
:::

The unit deviance is approximately a quadratic form for $y \approx \mu.$  

::: {#thm-devianceapprox}
For the unit deviance it holds that
$$d(y, \mu) = \frac{(y - \mu)^2}{\mathcal{V}(\mu)} + o((y - \mu)^2)$$
for $y, \mu \in J.$ 
:::

::: {.proof}
We consider the function 
$$
    y \mapsto d(y, \mu)
$$
around $\mu.$ Since we know that $d(\mu, \mu) = 0,$ that $y = \mu$ is a local minimum, and that $d$ is 
twice continuously differentiable in $J \times J,$ we get by Taylor's formula 
that
$$d(y, \mu) = \frac{1}{2} \partial_{y}^2 d(\mu, \mu) (y - \mu)^2 + o( (y - \mu)^2).$$
Using that $\partial_y \kappa(g(y)) = y g'(y)$ we find that 
$$
\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{2} \partial_{y}^2 d(y, \mu) & = \partial_{y}^2 \Big\{ y g(y) - \kappa(g(y)) - yg(\mu) + \kappa(g(\mu))\Big\} \\
& = \partial_{y} \Big\{ g(y) + y g'(y) - y g'(y) - g(\mu) \Big\}\\
& = g'(y) = \frac{1}{\kappa''(g(y))} = \frac{1}{\mathcal{V}(y)}.
\end{align*}
$$
Plugging in $y = \mu$ completes the proof.
:::

### Bregman divergences and quasi-deviances

There is a close connection between the unit deviances introduced above 
and the concept of Bregman divergences, which are general distance measures 
determined by convex functions. Indeed, the unit deviance is effectively 
twice the Bregman divergence determined by $\kappa$. 

::: {#def-bregman}
Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be an open interval and let $K : I \to \mathbb{R}$ 
be a continuously differentiable and strictly convex function. Then its associated 
Bregman divergence is defined by 
$$
    D_K(\theta, \theta_0) = K'(\theta_0)(\theta_0 - \theta) - K(\theta_0) + K(\theta)
$$
for $\theta, \theta_0 \in I.$
:::

Strict convexity of $K$ implies that $D_K(\theta, \theta_0) \geq 0$ and 
$D_K(\theta, \theta_0) = 0$ if and only if $\theta = \theta_0$. This 
justifies interpreting $D_K$ as a distance measure, though it is
neither symmetric nor does it fulfill the triangle inequality, so
$D_K$ is not a metric.

With $\theta = g(\mu)$ and $\theta_y = g(y)$ we see that 
$\kappa'(\theta_y) = g^{-1}(g(y)) = y$, and it then follows directly from @eq-exp-deviance that 
$$
    d(y, \mu) = 2 D_\kappa(\theta, \theta_y)
$$
in terms of the canonical parameters $\theta$ and $\theta_y$. 

For any twice continuously differentiable and strictly convex $K$, we can define
the quasi-link and quasi-variance functions by 
$$
    g_K(\mu) \coloneqq (K')^{-1}(\mu) \qquad \text{and} \qquad \mathcal{V}_K(\mu) \coloneqq K''(g_K(\mu))
$$
for $\mu \in J \coloneqq K'(I)$. Here we have used that strict convexity of $K$ implies that 
$K'$ is strictly increasing, whence has an inverse on $J$. Note that $J$ is an open interval. 

We can express the Bregman divergence given by $K$ in the mean value parametrization as 
$$
    d_K(y, \mu) \coloneqq 2 D_K(g_K(\mu), g_K(y))
$$
for $y, \mu \in J$. The following theorem gives a representation of any Bregman divergence 
in terms of its corresponding quasi-variance function.

::: {#thm-bregman-integral-rep}
With $\mathcal{V}_K$ a strictly positive quasi-variance function for a twice continuously 
differentiable and strictly convex $K$ it holds that 
$$
    d_K(y, \mu) = 2 \int_\mu^y \frac{y - t}{\mathcal{V}_K(t)} \mathrm{d} t
$$
for $y, \mu  \in J$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Using that $K'(g_K(y)) = y$, the definition of $d_K$ gives that 
$$
    d_K(y, \mu) = y(g_K(y) - g_K(\mu)) - K(g_K(y)) + K(g_K(\mu)). 
$$
Differentiation twice gives, exactly as in the proof of @thm-devianceapprox, that 
$$
    \frac{1}{2} \partial_{y}^2 d_K(y, \mu) = \frac{1}{\mathcal{V}_K(y)}.
$$
It then follows by integrating twice, and changing the order of integration, that
$$
     d_K(y, \mu) = 2 \int_{\mu}^y \int_\mu^s  \frac{1}{\mathcal{V}_K(t)} \mathrm{d} t \, \mathrm{d} s + ay + b
     = 2 \int_{\mu}^y  \frac{y - t}{\mathcal{V}_K(t)} \mathrm{d} t + ay + b.
$$
Since $\partial_y d_K(\mu, \mu) = d_K(\mu, \mu) = 0$ we conclude that $a = b = 0$.
:::

@exr-variance-to-bregman shows that *any* continuous
$\mathcal{V} : J \to (0, \infty)$, defined on an open interval $J$, is a 
quasi-variance function corresponding to Bregman divergence. The quasi-deviance,
defined by 
$$
    d(y, \mu) = 2 \int_\mu^y \frac{y - t}{\mathcal{V}(t)} \mathrm{d}t,
$$ {#eq-quasi-deviance}
equals twice the Bregman divergence by @thm-bregman-integral-rep and is 
identical to the deviance given by @eq-exp-deviance if $\mathcal{V}$ is 
the variance function for an exponential dispersion model. 

The upshot of this chapter is that for a (quasi-)variance function 
$\mathcal{V} : J \to \mathbb{R},$ specifying the relation between the 
mean and the variance of the outcome, there is a corresponding 
(quasi-)deviance, expressed by @eq-quasi-deviance, that can be used to 
quantify the deviation of the observation $y$ from the mean $\mu$. If 
the variance function happens to be the variance function of an 
exponential dispersion model, the deviance equals twice the negative 
log-likelihood up to an additive constant. And through the variance function 
a full probabilistic model of the outcome is specified in terms 
of the mean up to the dispersion parameter. Depending on what we want 
to achieve in practice, it may or may not be important to have a 
full probabilistic model, and @eq-quasi-deviance shows that only 
the mean-variance relation is actually needed to define the deviance. 


# Exercises  {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-bernoulli}
The probability mass function for any probability measure on $\{0, 1\}$ can be 
written as
$$p^y(1-p)^{1-y}$$
for $y \in \{0, 1\}.$ Show that this family of probability measures for $p \in (0,1)$ 
form an exponential family. Identify $I$ and how the canonical parameter depends 
on $p.$ 
:::

::: {#exr-binomial}
Show that the binomial distributions on $\{0, 1, \ldots, n\}$ with 
success probabilities $p \in (0,1)$ form an exponential family.
::: 

::: {#exr-deg}
 Show that if the structure measure $\nu = \delta_y$ is the Dirac-measure in $y$ 
then for the corresponding exponential family we have $P_{\theta} = \delta_y$ for all $\theta \in \mathbb{R}.$
Show next, that if $\nu$ is not a one-point measure, then 
$P_{\theta}$ is not a Dirac-measure for $\theta \in I$ and conclude that its
variance is strictly positive. 
::: 

::: {#exr-cum}
If $P$ is a probability measure on $\mathbb{R},$ its cumulant generating 
function is defined as the function
$$
    K(s) = \log \int e^{s y} \ P(\mathrm{d} y)
$$
for $s$ such that the integral is finite. Let $P_{\theta, \varphi}$ be an
exponential dispersion distribution with unit cumulant function $\kappa.$ Show that 
$$
    K_{\theta, \varphi}(s) =  \frac{\kappa(\theta + \varphi s) - \kappa(\theta)}{\varphi}
$$
is the cumulant generating function for $P_{\theta, \varphi}.$ 
:::

::: {#exr-uniqueness}
Let $P_{\theta}$ be the exponential family given by the structure measure $\nu.$ Show that 
$$
    \frac{\mathrm{d} \nu}{\mathrm{d} P_{\theta_0}} = e^{\kappa(\theta_0) - \theta y}
$$
for any $\theta_0 \in I.$ Then show that $\nu$ is uniquely specified by the unit cumulant 
function $\kappa.$ 

*Hint: Use that the cumulant generating function for $P_{\theta_0}$  is determined by $\kappa,$ and that a probability measure is uniquely determined by its cumulant generating function if it is defined on an open interval around $0.$*
::: 

::: {#exr-inverse-gauss}
This exercise is about the *inverse Gaussian distribution*, \index{inverse Gaussian distribution} 
which has density
$$
    f(y) = \sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{2 \pi y^3}} e^{-\frac{\lambda(y - \mu)^2}{2 \mu^2 y}}
$$ {#eq-invgaus}
w.r.t. Lebesgue measure on $(0, \infty).$ In this parametrization, $\lambda, \mu > 0$ are positive parameters. 

1.  Show that the family of inverse Gaussian distributions
    parametrized by $\lambda, \mu > 0$ is an exponential dispersion
    model. Identify how the canonical parameter and the dispersion
    parameter are given in terms of $\lambda$ and $\mu$---with the 
    lack of uniqueness resolved by letting the unit 
    structure measure correspond to $\lambda = 1.$
    [The use of $\mu$ in the "Wikipedia" parametrization in @eq-invgaus is sensible!]{.aside}
2.  Show that the mean is $\mu$ and show that the variance function is 
    $$
        \mathcal{V}(\mu) = \mu^3.
    $$
3.  Find the canonical link function and the unit deviance.
:::

::: {#exr-lebres}
This exercise is about the exponential family with structure measure 
$\nu = m_{[-1,1]}$ being Lebesgue measure restricted to the interval $[-1, 1].$ 

1. Compute the unit cumulant function $\kappa$ and show that
    $I = \mathbb{R}.$ Plot the density for the corresponding exponential
    family w.r.t. Lebesgue measure for $\theta = -1$ and $\theta = 1.$


Assume that $Y \sim P_{\theta}$ where 
$$
    \frac{\mathrm{d} P_{\theta}}{\mathrm{d} \nu} = e^{\theta y - \kappa(\theta)}.
$$

2. Compute the mean value function $\mu(\theta)$ and show that 
    $$
        \mathbf{V}(Y) = \frac{1}{\theta^2} - \frac{1}{\sinh(\theta)^2}
    $$
    for $\theta \neq 0.$ Plot the variance function $\mathcal{V}(\mu)$ as a function of $\mu.$ 

    *Hint: For the plot, it is not necessary to compute an analytic expression for the inverse of the mean value map.*
:::

::: {#exr-poisson-disp}

The unit cumulant function for the Poisson model is $\kappa(\theta) = e^\theta$, 
see @exm-pois. Let $S_\varphi(y) = \varphi y$ denote the scale transformation determined 
by $\varphi > 0$. 

1. Show that 
    $$
        \frac{\kappa(\theta)}{\varphi} = \log \int e^{\theta y} \bar{\nu}_\varphi(\mathrm{d} y)
        = \log \int e^{\frac{\theta y}{\varphi}} \nu_\varphi(\mathrm{d} y)
    $$
    with 
    $$
        \frac{\mathrm{d}\bar{\nu}_\varphi}{\mathrm{d} \tau} (y) = \frac{1}{\varphi^y y!}.
    $$
    and $\nu_\varphi = S_{\varphi}(\bar{\nu}_\varphi)$. 

2. Argue that the Poisson model in @exm-pois can be extended to an exponential dispersion 
    model where the support of the probability distribution $P_{\theta, \varphi}$ is 
    $\varphi \mathbb{N}_0$. 

3. Show that $S_{\varphi^{-1}}(P_{\theta, \varphi}) = \mathrm{Pois}(e^\theta / \varphi)$. That 
    is, $Y \sim \mathrm{Pois}(\mu / \varphi)$ if and only if $\varphi Y \sim \mathcal{E}(\log \mu, \nu_\varphi)$,
    which shows that the members of the exponential dispersion model are scaled Poisson distributions.

    *Hint: You can compute the probability mass function explicitly for the distribution $S_{\varphi^{-1}}(P_{\theta, \varphi})$ and identify it as the probability mass function for a Poisson distribution. Alternative, you can compute the cumulant generating function of $P_{\theta, \varphi}$ using @exr-cum and identify it as the cumulant generating function for a scaled Poisson distribution.* 

4. Compute $\mathbf{E}(\varphi Y)$ and $\mathbf{V}(\varphi Y)$ for $\varphi Y \sim \mathcal{E}(\log \mu, \nu_\varphi)$ directly, 
    using that $Y \sim \mathrm{Pois}(\mu / \varphi)$, and demonstrate that the results agree with @thm-meanvar.

::: 

::: {#exr-over-dispersion}

Let $N \sim \mathrm{Pois}(\mu_0)$ and let $Y_1, Y_2, \ldots \in \mathbb{N}_0$ be i.i.d. variables
independent of $N$ and with finite second moment. Define 
$$
    Y = \sum_{n=0}^{N} Y_n,
$$
whose distribution is a *compound Poisson distribution*. 

1. Show that $$\mu \coloneqq \mathbf{E}(Y) = \mathbf{E}(Y_1) \mu_0.$$ 
2. Show that $$\mathbf{V}(Y) = \frac{\mathbf{E}(Y_1^2)}{\mathbf{E}(Y_1)} \mu.$$
[This particular example is a distribution on the non-negative integers with the ratio $$\varphi = \frac{\mathbf{E}(Y_1^2)}{\mathbf{E}(Y_1)}$$ playing the role as a dispersion parameter.]{.aside}
::: 

::: {#exr-variance-to-bregman}

Let $J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be an open interval and let $\mathcal{V} : J \to (0, \infty)$ be continuous. 
Fix $\mu_0 \in J$ and define 
$$
    g(\mu) = \int_{\mu_0}^\mu \frac{1}{\mathcal{V}(t)} \mathrm{d} t.
$$

1. Show that $g$ is a strictly increasing and continuously differentiable function.


2. Argue that $I \coloneqq g(J)$ is open and use the inverse function theorem to conclude that $g^{-1}$ is 
   differentiable with 
   $$
        (g^{-1})'(\theta) = \mathcal{V}(g^{-1}(\theta)).
   $$

3. Let $\theta_0 = g(\mu_0)$ and show that 
   $$
        K(\theta) \coloneqq \int_{\theta_0}^\theta g^{-1}(s) \mathrm{d} s
   $$
   for $\theta \in I$ is twice continuously differentiable with 
   $$
        K''(\theta) = \mathcal{V}(g^{-1}(\theta)).
   $$

4. Argue that $K$ is strictly convex, and that its corresponding quasi-link and quasi-variance 
   functions are $g$ and $\mathcal{V}$, respectively. That is, $g_K = g$ and $\mathcal{V}_K = \mathcal{V}$.

:::
